But, in the instant case, even according to the 5th respondent, the collector had instructed the 3rd respondent - the District Revenue Officer to conduct the enquiry on 21.09.2010. In this regard, by inviting the attention of this Court to section 2(a) of the Act, the learned Senior Counsel submitted that "Collector" means the Collector appointed by the Government to perform the functions of the Collector under this Act. But, in the case on hand, absolutely no material to show that the District Revenue Officer - the 3rd respondent has been specifically appointed to perform the duty of the Collector. Under such circumstances, the non-hearing of the objections by the Collector himself directly is against the provisions of the Act and on that ground also, the impugned order is liable to be [LEAKAGE_MASK]. 12. The next fold of submission of the learned senior counsel for the petitioners is that under section 3(2) of the Act, the Government is empowered to issue notice for acquisition of land and under section 23-A of the said Act, the Government may delegate the powers to District Collectors, except certain powers mentioned in the said section, under G.O.Ms.No.513, Revenue (LAI(1), dated 02.09.2005. Under such circumstances, the Collector alone ought to have conducted the enquiry. The question of delegating powers further by the District Collector to some other person is not sustainable. Since the 3rd respondent conducted enquiry in favour of whom the Collector cannot delegate the power, the enquiry conducted by the 3rd respondent is not maintainable. 13. The learned senior counsel for the petitioners further submitted that as per Rule 6(c) of the Tamil Nadu Acquisition of Land for Industrial Purposes Rules, 2001, after filing objections by the pattadhars, the same have to be forwarded to the requisition body, namely, Airports Authority of India and thereafter, after receiving the remarks from the requisition body, necessary order has to be passed by the District Collector by considering the objections as well as the remarks of the requisition body. But, here, even without getting reply/remarks from the requisition body, the objections were disposed of, which is in violation of said Rule 6(c). That apart, each objector should be heard individually; but, in the instant case, mass enquiry was conducted. Learned senior counsel for the petitioners further submitted that as per the provisions of the Act , only the Collector has to conduct the enquiry. But, in the instant case, even according to the 5th respondent, the collector had instructed the 3rd respondent - the District Revenue Officer to conduct the enquiry on 21.09.2010. In this regard, by inviting the attention of this Court to section 2(a) of the Act, the learned Senior Counsel submitted that "Collector" means the Collector appointed by the Government to perform the functions of the Collector under this Act. But, in the case on hand, absolutely no material to show that the District Revenue Officer - the 3rd respondent has been specifically appointed to perform the duty of the Collector. Under such circumstances, the non-hearing of the objections by the Collector himself directly is against the provisions of the Act and on that ground also, the impugned order is liable to be [LEAKAGE_MASK]. 12. The next fold of submission of the learned senior counsel for the petitioners is that under section 3(2) of the Act, the Government is empowered to issue notice for acquisition of land and under section 23-A of the said Act, the Government may delegate the powers to District Collectors, except certain powers mentioned in the said section, under G.O.Ms.No.513, Revenue (LAI(1), dated 02.09.2005. Under such circumstances, the Collector alone ought to have conducted the enquiry. The question of delegating powers further by the District Collector to some other person is not sustainable. Since the 3rd respondent conducted enquiry in favour of whom the Collector cannot delegate the power, the enquiry conducted by the 3rd respondent is not maintainable. 13. The learned senior counsel for the petitioners further submitted that as per Rule 6(c) of the Tamil Nadu Acquisition of Land for Industrial Purposes Rules, 2001, after filing objections by the pattadhars, the same have to be forwarded to the requisition body, namely, Airports Authority of India and thereafter, after receiving the remarks from the requisition body, necessary order has to be passed by the District Collector by considering the objections as well as the remarks of the requisition body. But, here, even without getting reply/remarks from the requisition body, the objections were disposed of, which is in violation of said Rule 6(c). That apart, each objector should be heard individually; but, in the instant case, mass enquiry was conducted. The learned senior counsel further submitted that no individual notice was sent to the pattadhars, as requied under necessary rule. Thus, the learned counsel for the petitioners submitted that the entire enquiry is an empty formality. 14. The learned senior counsel for the petitioners submitted that it is the specific case of the petitioner in W.P.No.9004 of 2011 that in the land sought to be acquired, he already constructed a memorial building for his parents and the petitioner is regularly doing pooja in the said memorial; but the said objection was not considered. That apart, by inviting the attention of this Court to the sketch in the typed set, the learned senior counsel submitted that certain lands which are nearer to the present airport complex were not acquired, whereas the lands of the petitioners which are far away from the complex, have been notified in the notification, which would establish the pick and choose method adopted by the authorities in the acquisition process. In support of his contentions, A.Ramachandran vs The Secretary To Government on 13 March, 2013 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/55649087/ 8 the learned senior counsel has relied on a decision of this Court in the case of J.DORAIBABU .VS. STATE OF TAMIL NADU AND OTHERS (2011 W.L.R.505) wherein it has been held that the lock, stock and barrel rejection of the lawful objections raised by the land owners, by the District Collector, in the process of his undue haste in sending the report to the Government without considering the objections of the petitioners individually, vitiates the acquisition proceedings. Learned senior counsel further relied upon the decision reported in the case of HINDUSTAN PETROLEUM CORPORATION LTD., .vs. DARIUS SHAPUR CHENAI AND OTHERS reported in (2005) 7 SCC 627 for the same proposition. 17. Learned Additional Advocate General further submitted that it is incorrect to state that the enquiry was conducted by the District Revenue Officer. In fact, at the time of enquiry, the Collector went to the place of enquiry and conducted a meeting with the pattadhars and since the Collector was already pre-occupied with the other official work, he directed the District Revenue Officer to receive the objection petitions and thereafter, the District Collector himself passed the impugned order after considering the reply sent by the requisition body on 02.11.2010. Under such circumstances, no infirmity could be found in the impugned order passed by the District Collector and, as such, the writ petitions are liable to be dismissed. In support of his contentions, the learned Additional Advocate General has relied on the decisions reported in FRIENDS COLONY DEVELOPMENT COMMITTEE .vs. STATE OF ORISSA AND OTHERS (AIR 2005 SC 1), A.Ramachandran vs The Secretary To Government on 13 March, 2013 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/55649087/ 9 Md.MURTAZA & OTHERS .vs. STATE OF ASSAM & OTHERS (2012 AIR SCW 189), UNION OF INDIA .vs. DR.KUSHALA SHETTY AND OTHERS (2011 AIR SC 3210) and AVISHEK GOENKA .vs. UNION OF INDIA AND ANOTHER (2012(4) SCALE 602). 18. In this regard, learned senior counsel has also invited the attention of this Court to section 23-A of the Act and submitted that under section 23-A, delegation was given by the Government only to the District Collector to conduct the enquiry and as per section 2(a) of the Act, "Collector" means the Collector of a District, and includes any officer specifically appointed by the Government to perform the functions of the Collector under this Act.
texts.respondent_arguments: 15. Learned Additional Advocate General appearing for respondents 1 to 3 submitted that totally 585.98 acres of land was sought to be acquired by the Airport Authority of India. Out of which, 4.64 acres were poramboke land. The extent of 581.34 acres of land to be acquired were owned by 1086 persons and only 6 persons were objecting the acquisition proceedings and the Government has received 389 objections. Out of 586 acres, 33.9 acres alone is in dispute. These lands were sought to be required for acquisition of Tuticorin Airport. Acquisition is made only as per the Master plan of the Airport Authority of India. Therefore, it is incorrect to state that the respondents are adopting pick and choose method in acquiring the lands. The learned Additional Advocate General, by inviting the attention of this Court to the objections filed by each of the petitioners, has elaborately demonstrated that all the objections were considered properly by the District Collector and thereafter only, the impugned order has been passed. It is incorrect to state that in W.P.No.9004 of 2011, there has been an memorial in the lands sought to be acquired. In the inspection report of the Collector, no mention was made to the existence of memorial and if at all any memorial building is in existence in the said land, it should have been constructed only after initiation of acquisition proceedings. 19. It is the main submission of the learned senior counsel for the petitioners that the notification under section 3(2) of the Act was published only on 28.08.2010 and as per which, 30 days' time was given to the pattadhars to give objection. But, before expiry of 30 days, the enquiry was conducted. Therefore, since the enquiry was conducted before the expiry of 30 days, the entire land acquisition proceedings is vitiated.
texts.other_lawyer_arguments: In 2011 AIR SC 3210 (supra), the Hon'ble Apex Court has held that when a particular project is found to be opposed to the mandate of law or tainted due to mala fide, only in that case the Court can nullify the acquisition of land and not otherwise. The relevant paragraph reads as follows: "24. Therefore, the order under challenge cannot be sustained". 25. In AIR 2005 SC 1 (supra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held as under: "22. In all developed and developing countries there is emphasis on planned development of cities which is sought to be achieved by zoning, planning and regulating building construction activity. Such planning, though highly complex, is a matter based on scientific research, study and experience leading to rationalization of laws by way of legislative enactments and rules and regulations framed thereunder. Zoning and planning do result in hardship to individual property owners as their freedom to use their property in the way they like, is subjected to regulation and control. The private owners are to some extent prevented from making the most profitable use of their property. But for this reason alone the controlling regulations cannot be termed as arbitrary or unreasonable. The private interest stands subordinated to the public good. It can be stated in a way that power to plan development of city and to regulate the building activity therein flows from the police power of the state. The exercise of such governmental power is justified on account of its being reasonably necessary for the public health, safety, morals or general welfare and ecological considerations; though an unnecessary or unreasonable inter- meddling with the private ownership of the property may not be justified". 26. In 2012 AIR SCW 189 (supra) , it has been held by the Supreme Court as under: "7.Ordinarily everywhere in the world wholesale markets are situated at the outskirts or outside the city limits. No doubt, the shifting of the shops of the wholesellers will cause some hardships to some individuals, but it is well settled that public interest prevails over the private interests. Thus, in Friends Colony Development Committee vs. State of Orissa AIR 2005 SC 1 (vide para 22) this Court observed : "The private interest stands subordinated to the public good.". A.Ramachandran vs The Secretary To Government on 13 March, 2013 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/55649087/ 13 ......... 13. It must be remembered that certain matters are by their very nature such as had better be left to the administrative authorities instead of Courts themselves seeking to substitute their own views and perceptions as to what is the best solution to the problem. In matters of policy the Courts have a limited role and it should only interfere with the same when it is clearly illegal. The impugned action is a salutary step for undoing a mischief, which was crying out for redress for a long time, and it is not illegal." 27. In 2012 (4) SCALE 602, it has been held by the Supreme Court that the public welfare should prevail as the highest law and private interest would stand subordinate to public good. The relevant paragraphs are extracted hereunder: 19. The legislative intent attaching due significance to the 'public safety' is evident from the object and reasons of the Act, the provisions of the Act and more particularly, the Rules framed thereunder. Use of these black films have been proved to be criminal's paradise and a social evil. If these crimes can be reduced by enforcing the prohibition of law, it would further the cause of Rule of Law and Public Interest as well. 20. This Court in the case of Hira Tikoo v. Union Territory of Chandigarh [(2004) 6 SCC 765], while dealing with the provisions of town planning and the land allotted to the allottees, upon which the allotees had made full payment, held that such allotment was found to be contravening other statutory provisions and the allotted area was situated under the reserved forest land and land in periphery of 900 meters of Air Force Base. The Court held that there was no vested right and public welfare should prevail as the highest law. Thus, this Court, while relying upon the maxim "salus populi est suprema lex", modified the order of the High Court holding that the allottees had no vested right and the land forming part of the forest area could not be taken away for other purposes. Reference can also be made to the judgment of this Court in Friends Colony Development Committee v. State of Orissa [AIR 2005 SC 1], where this Court, while referring to construction A.Ramachandran vs The Secretary To Government on 13 March, 2013 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/55649087/ 14 activity violative of the regulations and control orders, held that the regulations made under Orissa Development Authorities Act, 1982 may meddle with private rights but still they cannot be termed arbitrary or unreasonable. The private interest would stand subordinate to public good. 21. In the present case as well, even if some individual interests are likely to suffer, such individual or private interests must give into the larger public interest. It is the duty of all citizens to comply with the law. The Rules are mandatory and nobody has the authority in law to mould these rules for the purposes of convenience or luxury and certainly not for crime. We may also note that a Bench of this Court, vide its Order dated 15th December, 1998 in Civil Appeal No. 3700 of 1999 titled Chandigarh Administration and Others v. Namit Kumar & Ors., had permitted the use of 'light coloured tinted glasses' only while specifically disapproving use of films on the vehicles. Subsequently, in the same case, but on a different date, another Bench of this Court vide its order reported at [(2004) 8 SCC 446] made a direction that mandate of sub-Rule (2) of Rule 100 shall be kept in mind while dealing with such cases."
